speaker: Doctor
text: Welcome to the clinic. I see you are experiencing episodes of dizziness and vertigo; to help me understand your condition better, how long do these episodes last, and do they occur when you change your head position?

speaker: Patient
text: 70-year-old woman. The patient presents with sudden episodes of dizziness that are position dependent. She describes experiencing a false sensation of motion and occasional spinning, indicative of vertigo. She denies any recent illnesses, injuries, or significant changes in health status, apart from age-related hearing loss (presbycusis).

speaker: Doctor

The fact that your dizziness is position-dependent and involves a spinning sensation is very specific; do you notice any associated symptoms like nausea, vomiting, or ringing in your ears (tinnitus)? Also, have you experienced any recent sudden loss of hearing in one ear?

speaker: Measurement
text: RESULTS: Bilateral high-frequency sensorineural hearing loss, consistent with presbycusis. No sudden drops in hearing indicative of Meniere's disease or labyrinthitis.

speaker: Doctor
text: Thank you. The combination of position-dependent vertigo in a 70-year-old woman with presbycusis strongly suggests a vestibular origin. Have you noticed any visual blurring or diplopia (double vision) during these spells, and is the nystagmus (eye movement) unidirectional? REQUEST TEST: Dix-Hallpike Maneuver.

speaker: Measurement
text: RESULTS: Positive for right-sided horizontal nystagmus when moving from sitting to supine position, suggestive of BPPV.

speaker: Doctor
text:
DIAGNOSIS READY: Benign Paroxysmal Positional Vertigo (BPPV) of the right posterior canal.

The positive Dix-Hallpike maneuver with right-sided horizontal nystagmus confirms your diagnosis. I will now arrange for you to undergo canalith repositioning maneuvers (Epley maneuver) to treat this condition.
